cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/0/t: Vatican II brought the vernacular Mass worldwide, and mainline Protestants converged on shared lectionaries and Eucharistic practice. Pentecostal-charismatic praise and worship, with bands and extended singing, became the dominant style in much of the global South; streaming services spread after 2020.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/1/t: Taizé chants, Vineyard, Hillsong and Bethel worship songs circulate globally; African, Latin American and Asian Christians compose in local idioms. Gospel and Christian contemporary music became major industries, while traditional chant and choirs persisted.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/2/t: Megachurches in Seoul, Lagos, São Paulo and Texas built arenas with stages, screens and campuses; Nigeria's Redemption Camp holds millions. Catholic churches reoriented altars toward the people; Orthodox churches rebuilt thousands of churches across the former Soviet Union.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/3/t: Christian art now depicts Christ in African, Asian and Indigenous forms; icons are widely revived in the West. Film, television and digital media have become major vehicles of Christian imagery.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/4/t: Taizé (1940), the Missionaries of Charity (1950), Bose and charismatic covenant communities offered new forms of common life. Orthodox monasticism revived on Athos and in Russia, Romania and Ethiopia, while Western religious orders shrank.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/5/t: Ecumenical efforts to agree a common date for Easter continue, especially around the 1700th anniversary of Nicaea (2025). Christians widely observe Advent and Lent again, and new commemorations (Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, Reformation 500 in 2017) reflect ecumenism.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/6/t: Many Protestant churches ordain women; Anglican provinces debate women bishops (first in 1989); Catholic and Orthodox churches reserve priesthood to men. Women form the majority of active Christians worldwide and lead many Pentecostal and African churches.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/7/t: Seminaries and universities in Africa, Asia and Latin America produce theologians shaping world Christianity (Bediako, Gutiérrez, Koyama). Online learning and Bible apps (e.g., YouVersion) transform access.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/8/t: Christianity's centre of gravity has shifted south: by 2020 Africa had more Christians than any other continent. Korean, Brazilian and Nigerian missionaries serve worldwide, and migrant churches reshape Europe and North America.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/9/t: Communist regimes in China, North Korea and the Soviet bloc persecuted believers; Latin American martyrs included Romero; jihadist violence devastated Christians in Iraq, Syria and northern Nigeria. Ecumenical commemoration of 'new martyrs' unites traditions.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/10/: After the Holocaust, Nostra Aetate (1965) and Protestant statements repudiated deicide charges and antisemitism; John Paul II visited Rome's synagogue (1986). Messianic Jewish congregations and Christian Zionism generate fresh debate.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/11/: Christian–Muslim dialogue (A Common Word, 2007; Abu Dhabi Document, 2019) coexists with conflict and emigration of Middle Eastern Christians. Large numbers of Muslim-background believers are reported in Iran and Algeria, and Christian–Muslim relations shape Nigeria, Egypt and Indonesia.
cultures/culture-contemporary/panels/12/: Western Europe secularised rapidly, while Christianity revived in post-Soviet Russia with close state ties. China's state regulates churches, and Christian nationalism, liberation theology and religious-freedom advocacy all shape politics.
